intro: How much income Australian residents can earn before paying income tax, how to claim the threshold from an employer, and how it works for part of a year.
explanation:
## Only Australian residents for tax purposes can claim it

The tax-free threshold is available to people who are Australian residents for tax purposes. A person who is a non-resident for the whole year cannot claim it and is taxed on all of their Australian income. A resident for only part of the year gets a smaller, part-year threshold in place of the full amount. Tax residency is a separate test from immigration status, so a person can be a resident for tax purposes without being a citizen or permanent resident, and can hold a visa without being a resident.

## Claiming it reduces the tax withheld from your pay

When you start with a payer, you complete a **tax file number (TFN) declaration**, and that form is where you choose whether to claim the threshold. A payer can be an employer or a government agency such as Centrelink. If you choose not to claim it, more tax is withheld. The threshold applies to your income across an **income year**, which runs from 1 July to 30 June.

## With more than one payer, you generally claim it from only one

Where several payers pay you in the same period, the threshold generally goes with just one of them, usually the best-paying. Claiming it from every payer can leave too little tax withheld when your total income is above {fact:au_tax_free_threshold}, and you may get a tax bill for the difference. You can claim it from each payer only if you are certain your total income from all of them will be {fact:au_tax_free_threshold} or less. If it later rises above that, you need to tell a payer to stop applying it. Moving to a different employer lets you claim it there too, even if you claimed it with the last one.

Your tax return is where the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) sets all your income against the tax already withheld. If more was withheld than you owed, a refund can follow, and if less, a bill.
